title: Rocky 'Super-Earth' 49 Light-Years Away Shows First Signs of Atmosphere, Boosting Search for Alien Life
excerpt: Scientists have detected helium escaping from LHS 1140b, a rocky planet in the habitable zone of its star, making it the strongest candidate yet for an atmosphere on an Earth-like world beyond our solar system.
body:
• Scientists detected helium escaping from exoplanet LHS 1140b, a rocky super-Earth 49 light-years from Earth, suggesting it has an atmosphere.
  • If confirmed, it would be the first atmosphere detected on a rocky planet in the habitable zone of another star.
  • The planet is about five times Earth's mass and orbits a red dwarf star at the right distance for liquid water to exist.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, will be followed up with observations from the James Webb Space Telescope and ground-based observatories.

Scientists say they have detected the strongest evidence yet that a rocky planet orbiting a star 49 light-years from Earth possesses an atmosphere — a finding that, if confirmed, would mark a milestone in the search for extraterrestrial life and make the planet a prime target for future investigation.

The planet, called LHS 1140b, is classified as a "super-Earth" at about five times our planet's mass. It orbits within the habitable zone of its star, where surface temperatures could allow liquid water to exist. Researchers detected helium escaping from around the planet, confirming the presence of an atmospheric envelope.

"I think it's the best place to look for life outside the solar system at this point. It's mostly rocky, it's at the right temperature to support liquid water on the surface, and it has an atmosphere — those are the three key ingredients we look for."

— Collin Cherubim, NASA Sagan Fellow, University of Chicago

From Theory to Detection

The discovery, published July 16 in the journal Science, was led by Collin Cherubim, a NASA Sagan Fellow at the University of Chicago who conducted the research during his doctoral work at Harvard University.

Cherubim first developed a theoretical model predicting that some rocky planets would retain helium atmospheres. As planets evolve from gas-rich formations into rocky bodies, they lose their lighter hydrogen but can hold onto slightly heavier helium. He then used the Magellan Clay telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile to search for the telltale gas.

In September 2024, he found it — helium escaping from LHS 1140b.

"Collin analyzed the planets we knew about and predicted that this one would have a helium atmosphere," said David Charbonneau, head of the Harvard Department of Astronomy. "Then he organized telescope time, got the data, and the detection was statistically rock-solid."

A Planet in the Sweet Spot

LHS 1140b orbits a red dwarf star, the most common stellar type in the universe. Because red dwarfs are smaller and cooler than sun-like stars, it is easier to study the atmospheres of their planets. However, red dwarfs are also volatile, emitting intense X-ray and ultraviolet radiation that can strip atmospheres away entirely.

The fact that LHS 1140b appears to have retained its atmosphere for more than three billion years makes it especially significant. "Can rocky planets have atmospheres around red dwarfs? This is the first bona fide yes," Cherubim said.

Helium alone would not support life, but scientists hope it may be accompanied by other gases such as oxygen or water vapor that have not yet been detected.

A Mystery to Resolve

In a follow-up observation in 2025, the team did not detect helium again. The researchers attribute this to natural variability in the rate of helium escape, which may have dipped below their instrument's sensitivity threshold. Cherubim acknowledged the gap: "That's a big mystery right now that we're very actively thinking about."

Michaël Gillon, research director at Belgium's University of Liège, called the study exciting but urged caution. "The helium signal was detected only once and was absent in follow-up observations," he said. "Before drawing conclusions, there is a need to establish that the signal is genuinely associated with the planet and reproducible."

What Comes Next

Multiple major observatories are set to train their instruments on LHS 1140b. The James Webb Space Telescope, the Hubble Space Telescope, and additional ground-based facilities in Chile will all observe the planet in coming months.

Study coauthor Jason Dittmann, who led the team that first discovered LHS 1140b in 2017, said the attention is well deserved. "It's like my little planet is all grown up now," he said. "If I had to put money down right now, I'd say this is the first of, if not many, then several. And it'll be really exciting to compare these planets to each other."
